title: Not to divide
hookLine: what he hears here he does not repeat there to set people apart (DN 1)
last: THE MIRROR — LOOK IN THE MIRROR.

cards: It starts so innocently. Can I tell you something? Don't say I said this.
And then a sentence moves from one room to another, from one friend to the next, and arrives a little bigger than it left.
By the end of the week, two people who used to get lunch together aren't speaking, and neither is quite sure why. It can happen in an office, a family, a group chat.
The sutta that opens the Long Discourses has a line about exactly this.

teach.b: The sutta is the Brahmajala, the all-embracing net, and near its start it lists what an ordinary person might praise in the Buddha. Several of the items are about speech.
One is about pisuṇā vācā, divisive speech, the second of the four guards. And the description is precise.
What he hears in one place, he doesn't repeat in another to set people there against the people here. What he hears there, he doesn't repeat here. That's the mechanism of gossip, named exactly.
Information isn't the problem. Carrying it in order to split people is. The sutta doesn't stop at refusing.
It turns the guard into a job. In T. W.
Rhys Davids's translation, he lives "as a binder together of those who are divided, an encourager of those who are friends".
The passage goes on to call him a peacemaker who speaks words that make for peace. So this guard has two halves: don't carry the sentence that splits, and when you can, carry the sentence that mends.
No vows, no robes. Just what you do with something you heard by the coffee machine. Over time, people tend to notice who repeats things, and who doesn't.
The tradition takes it seriously enough to put it in two places: here on the path, and in the monks' own code, which has a specific offense for tale-bearing between monks.

how: Buddhists treat abstaining from divisive speech as part of right speech; monastics keep a rule against tale-bearing among monks, and some teachers suggest simply letting gossip stop with you.

o: speech that's rude or crude in tone
words carried to split people apart

games.q: what's inside not dividing: tap the pairs.
p: first sutta of the Long Discourses

s: the sutta's concern is only whether the gossip is true
the concern is purpose: words carried from one side to the other to set people apart.
the Brahmajala also names the positive side: a peacemaker
it calls him a binder together of the divided and a speaker of words that make for peace.
monks have a specific rule against tale-bearing between monks
it's an offense in the monastic code, alongside the path factor of right speech.

games.q: a friend leans in: "don't tell anyone, but Sam said your idea was dumb." what does the Brahmajala picture?
o: pass it on to Sam's other friends.
let it stop with you, and look for a way to mend.
confront Sam in front of everyone.
games.why: DN 1 describes the Buddha as not carrying words from there to here to set people apart, and as a binder together of those who are divided.

practice: Think of something you heard recently about someone, the kind of thing that travels, and notice the small pull to pass it on. Don't fight it; just feel it, and let it sit there.
Then picture the two people it would land between, still speaking, still getting lunch, and rest in the quiet of a sentence not carried.

wordCard.voice: Pisuna vaca, divisive speech. In the first of the Long Discourses, the Buddha doesn't carry words to split people; he binds together those who are divided.

orig.note: Pali pisuṇā vācā: divisive or slanderous speech, the second of the four kinds right speech gives up.

carryVoice: Your line: a sentence that mends. Heard here, and not repeated there. Until next time.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 1 (Brahmajala Sutta), the section on slander
sources.work: Dialogues of the Buddha, part I
sources.q: as a binder together of those who are divided, an encourager of those who are friends
